summary.text: The Reign of Terror was a period of the French Revolution, after the First Republic was created, when massacres and numerous public executions took place.
These killings came in response to Federalist revolts, revolutionary fervour, anticlerical sentiment, and accusations of treason by the Committee of Public Safety.
It ended in July 1794 with the fall of Robespierre in the Thermidorian Reaction, by which time 16,594 official death sentences had been given.

facts.value: An estimated ten to twenty thousand executed or died in prison

facts.label: How it ended
facts.value: With the fall of Robespierre in July 1794

items.prompt: In Robespierre's view, what had to happen before France could have a republic built for the shared interests of everyone?

options.label: The king had to be allowed to share in governing
Every faction had to be given a seat in the Convention
Those who fought against that ideal had to be expelled
The foreign monarchies had to be invited to negotiate

items.explain: Robespierre felt the Revolution could produce a republic built for the general will, but only once those who fought against the ideal were expelled.

items.prompt: Robespierre thought the French people lacked virtue, which Montesquieu defined as the love of laws and country. What did he decide to do?

options.label: Weed out those he believed could never have it
Teach it to the people in free public schools
Reward the towns that showed the most of it
Ask foreign rulers to judge who had it

items.explain: Because he believed the virtue needed for democracy was lacking, he decided to weed out those who could never possess it.

items.prompt: How did the war with foreign powers help justify the Terror?

options.label: Foreign powers had demanded harsh punishments from France
Leaders saw terror as linked to victory, and the pressure to succeed justified their actions
The war had ended, so leaders had free time to try suspects
Soldiers had refused to fight until the traitors were gone

items.explain: Leaders saw a link between using terror and winning, and the pressure to succeed in the struggle justified their actions.

items.prompt: Austria and Prussia's leaders said they would restore Louis XVI if other rulers joined them. How did France respond?

options.label: It restored the king to power to avoid a conflict
It asked other rulers to arbitrate the dispute
It sent officers to negotiate a treaty with them
It declared war, viewing their statement as foreign meddling

items.explain: France declared war in response to what it viewed as the meddling of foreign powers.

options.label: The Montagnards
The Girondins
The First Coalition

items.explain: The Girondins were more conservative, while the Montagnards supported radical violence and pressures of the lower classes.

options.label: It began the moment the Directory took power in France

paragraphs.heading: What the Terror was
paragraphs.text: The Reign of Terror, in French La Terreur, was a stretch of the French Revolution that came after the First Republic was founded. During it, a series of massacres and many public executions took place. They answered several pressures at once: the Federalist revolts, the heat of revolutionary feeling, hostility to the Church, and charges of treason brought by the Committee of Public Safety. The Convention never made terror an official legal policy; it worked more as an idea.

paragraphs.heading: When it began and ended
paragraphs.text: Historians do not agree on when the Terror started. Some place it in 1793, often naming 5 September or 10 March, tied to the moment the Revolutionary Tribunal came into being. Others reach back to the September Massacres of 1792, or even to July 1789, when the revolution saw its first killing. Will Durant argued that, strictly speaking, it ran from the Law of Suspects in September 1793 until Robespierre was executed on 28 July 1794. It ended with the fall of Robespierre and his alleged allies that July, an episode known as the Thermidorian Reaction.

paragraphs.heading: The human cost
paragraphs.text: By the time it ended, 16,594 official death sentences had been handed down across France since June 1793. Of those, 2,639 were in Paris. On top of that, an estimated ten to twenty thousand more people were executed without a trial or died in prison while waiting for one.

paragraphs.heading: The ideas behind it
paragraphs.text: The leaders of the Terror drew on Enlightenment thought, which prized reason and had started to question the legal and moral footing of society. Jean-Jacques Rousseau's Social Contract held that people are born with rights and join together to form a government that protects them. Such a government had to serve the general will, meaning the interests of everyone rather than of a few factions. Robespierre took from this that the Revolution could build a republic for the general will, but only after its opponents were driven out. Anyone who resisted was branded a tyrant, and the leaders, seeing threats both inside and outside France, believed terror was the only way to keep the republic's dignity.

paragraphs.heading: A republic of virtue
paragraphs.text: Robespierre was also shaped by another Enlightenment writer, Baron de Montesquieu. In The Spirit of Law, Montesquieu named virtue, which he called the love of the laws and of one's country, as a core principle of democratic government. Speaking to the National Convention on 5 February 1794, Robespierre called virtue the basic principle of popular government. He believed the French people sorely lacked it, so he set out to weed out those he thought could never have it, which kept pushing the country toward terror. The Convention used this to justify its call to crush the revolution's enemies and save liberty.

paragraphs.heading: War and fear
paragraphs.text: War gave the Terror much of its urgency. In August 1791 Leopold II of Austria and Frederick William II of Prussia issued the Pillnitz Declaration, offering to restore the French king if other European rulers joined them, and France declared war on 20 April 1792. Many early battles were clear French defeats, and Austro-Prussian forces advanced on Paris. Those losses, together with uprisings at home, pushed the government toward drastic steps to make sure every citizen was loyal to the revolution. Even after a key victory at Valmy in September 1792, the pressure of the war served as a justification, and Albert Soboul summed it up: terror began as an improvised answer to defeat and, once organized, became a tool for winning.

paragraphs.heading: Pressure from the streets
paragraphs.text: The Convention itself was bitterly split between the Girondins, its more conservative leaders, and the Montagnards, who backed radical violence and the demands of the lower classes. Outside, the sans-culottes, the urban workers of France, joined the Hébertists in pressing the delegates. Once the Montagnards took control they called for radical measures, while the sans-culottes held violent demonstrations demanding punishment for anyone who opposed the interests of the poor.
